title: Ἀηδὼν καὶ ἱέραξ
part: The Nightingale and the Hawk (Chambry 8 · Perry 4)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 8 (= Perry 4). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », [ ] for words Chambry deletes as interpolated). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀηδὼν ἐπί τινος ὑψηλῆς δρυὸς καθημένη κατὰ τὸ σύνηθες ᾖδεν.
sentences.tr: Aēdōn epi tinos hypsēlēs dryos kathēmenē kata to synēthes ēiden.
sentences.l: A nightingale, sitting on a certain lofty oak, was singing according to her custom.
sentences.n: κατὰ τὸ σύνηθες: a neuter adjective made into a noun by the article, “according to the customary” — the standard Greek way of saying “as usual.” ᾖδεν is the imperfect of ᾄδω, holding the song open until the hawk arrives.

sentences.t: Ἱέραξ δὲ αὐτὴν θεασάμενος, ὡς ἠπόρει τροφῆς, ἐπιπτὰς συνέλαβεν.
sentences.tr: Hierax de autēn theasamenos, hōs ēporei trophēs, epiptas synelaben.
sentences.l: And a hawk, having beheld her — since he was in want of food — having flown upon her, seized her.
sentences.i: A hawk caught sight of her and, being short of food, swooped and seized her.
sentences.n: ὡς here is causal, “since”; it will also turn up meaning “when” and “that,” and only the sentence decides which. ἀπορέω takes the genitive of what is lacking: τροφῆς, “in want of food.”

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ μέλλουσα ἀναιρεῖσθαι ἐδέετο αὐτοῦ μεθεῖναι αὐτήν, λέγουσα ὡς οὐχ ἱκανή ἐστιν ἱέρακος αὐτὴ γαστέρα πληρῶσαι· δεῖ δὲ αὐτόν, εἰ τροφῆς ἀπορεῖ, ἐπὶ τὰ μείζονα τῶν ὀρνέων τρέπεσθαι.
sentences.tr: Hē de mellousa anaireisthai edeeto autou metheinai autēn, legousa hōs ouch hikanē estin hierakos autē gastera plērōsai: dei de auton, ei trophēs aporei, epi ta meizona tōn orneōn trepesthai.
sentences.l: And she, being about to be killed, was begging him to let her go, saying that she by herself was not enough to fill a hawk's belly, and that he must, if he is in want of food, turn to the larger of the birds.
sentences.i: As she was about to be killed she begged him to release her, saying that she alone was not enough to fill a hawk's belly, and that if he was short of food he should turn to the larger birds.
sentences.n: ὡς after a verb of saying introduces reported speech exactly as ὅτι does. δέομαι takes the genitive of the person asked (αὐτοῦ) with an infinitive of the request. The ὡς-clause runs on into a second limb with δέ (δεῖ δὲ αὐτόν) without repeating ὡς — δεῖ is a finite indicative like ἐστιν before it, and αὐτόν keeps the third person, so this is still her speech reported, not quoted.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὃς ὑποτυχὼν εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’ ἔγωγε ἀπόπληκτος ἂν εἴην, εἰ τὴν ἐν χερσὶν ἑτοίμην βορὰν παρεὶς τὰ μηδέπω φαινόμενα διώκοιμι. »
sentences.tr: Kai hos hypotychōn eipen: « All’ egōge apoplēktos an eiēn, ei tēn en chersin hetoimēn boran pareis ta mēdepō phainomena diōkoimi. »
sentences.l: And he, taking-up-the-word, said: « But I should be out of my senses, if, letting go the ready food in my hands, I were to chase the things not yet appearing. »
sentences.i: The hawk broke in and said, « I should be out of my senses to let go the meal already in my grip and chase what is not yet even in sight. »
sentences.n: ὑποτυχών is not “having taken hold of” but ὑποτυγχάνω, “take up the word, reply” — the collection's regular way of marking an answer. καὶ ὅς, “and he,” preserves an old use of ὅς as a demonstrative rather than a relative; it survives in narrative formulas like this one. εἴην … διώκοιμι are optatives with ἄν — the future-less-vivid condition, “should I …, I would …”, a supposition held at arm's length. ἐν χερσίν, “in the hands,” is the ordinary idiom for what one already has hold of; it is used unchanged here even though the speaker is a bird.

sentences.t: Οὕτως καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀλόγιστοί εἰσιν οἱ δι’ ἐλπίδα μειζόνων [πραγμάτων] τὰ ἐν χερσὶν ὄντα προΐενται.
sentences.tr: Houtōs kai tōn anthrōpōn alogistoi eisin hoi di’ elpida meizonōn [pragmatōn] ta en chersin onta proientai.
sentences.l: So too, of men, senseless are those who through hope of greater [things] let go the things that are in their hands.
sentences.i: So too those men are senseless who, in hope of greater things, let slip what they already hold.
sentences.n: Square brackets are Chambry's mark for words he judges a later insertion and deletes, though he prints them so the reader can see the seam — this text is a reconstruction and we show it as one. οἱ with a finite verb (προΐενται) is doing a relative's work, “those who” — the article standing in for the relative, a usage this later Greek allows. The closing echoes the hawk's own words, τὰ ἐν χερσίν.
